messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan is a 42-year-old South Asian man who works as a tax inspector, married with two children, and presents with a PCL-5 score of 72 following an incident approximately fourteen months ago in which he accidentally struck a cyclist while pulling out of a car park adjacent to his district office. The cyclist, a young man, sustained a fractured pelvis and severe head trauma and spent several weeks in intensive care. He survived, but with lasting neurological impairment. Rajan was not charged, and colleagues at the revenue office told him repeatedly that it was an accident, that the sun had been in his eyes, that anyone might have done the same. None of this reached him. From the moment he climbed out of his car and saw the man lying in the road, something in Rajan's understanding of himself and his world broke open in a way that has not closed since.

The event itself left a fractured imprint. Rajan can describe certain moments with painful, almost photographic clarity — the sound of the impact, a low thud followed by a scrape he still hears in quiet rooms — but other stretches of those minutes are simply gone, as though the film reel was cut. He does not know exactly how long he stood before calling for help. He is not sure what he said when he knelt beside the man. These gaps are not a relief to him; they are, he says, a source of dread. He had come to believe that the missing pieces must contain something worse than what he can remember — some hesitation, some failure of instinct — and this conviction feeds directly into his sense of himself as a man who, when it mattered, failed to protect another human being. The fragmented memory does not soften the horror; it amplifies his appraisals of his own culpability, and those appraisals in turn seem to sharpen the clarity of the worst moments while leaving the exculpatory details buried. The auditory echo of the impact, in particular, surfaces without warning and makes the scene feel immediate and present, pulling him back before he has chosen to return.

When the intrusions come — triggered most acutely by the sight of cars in collision, even minor fender-benders he passes on the road to his office, or by any encounter with funerals, cemeteries, or the language of grief — Rajan reaches immediately for a set of mental strategies that have become as automatic as flinching. He tells himself he deserves to suffer, that self-punishment is the only honest response to what he has done. He reminds himself, with a kind of grim accounting, that the man lived, that it could have been a fatality, that he should be grateful. He pushes the thoughts down with effort, sometimes spending entire audit reviews mentally suppressing the image of the cyclist's body. These strategies feel, to Rajan, like moral seriousness. In practice, they sustain and deepen his sense of permanent humiliation — the feeling that he is marked, that everyone who knows what happened sees the same thing he sees when he looks in the mirror. The self-punishment thinking in particular forecloses any revision of his beliefs about himself, and the downward comparisons, rather than providing relief, seem to circle back and reactivate the imagery he is trying to contain, so that the very act of reminding himself it could have been worse conjures again the crash, the sound, the road.

His beliefs about how the world works — that care and attention keep others safe, that a decent man does not destroy a stranger's life on an ordinary Tuesday — have not recovered. He avoids any conversation about the event at work, and when a colleague once mentioned a road accident in passing, Rajan excused himself and did not return for the rest of the afternoon. Over the months this withdrawal has become noticeable; his manager has commented on his distraction during fieldwork that requires him to drive between client sites, and his wife has described him as absent even when present.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was an invitation to a colleague's father's funeral — a routine, expected social obligation — which he could not bring himself to attend. He told his wife he was unwell. He has come to therapy not because he believes he can be helped, but because he is afraid that if he continues as he is, he will lose what remains of the life he had before that Tuesday. What he most fears, he said quietly in the first session, is that he already has.
